summary: This informational RFC reviews the privacy and security trade-offs of different ways to generate IPv6 addresses, including both standardized and non-standardized methods. It looks at which threats each method helps with, such as tracking a device across networks, and what implementers and users give up when choosing one.

plainLanguage.summary: The part of an IPv6 address that identifies an interface can reveal whether the same device is connecting from different places. RFC 7721 compares address-generation methods and the privacy and operational trade-offs they create.

subtitle: How IPv6 interface-identifier choices affect tracking, scanning, and device profiling.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 address includes an interface identifier, and some ways of generating it expose a stable hardware identifier. Observers can use that identifier to correlate activity, track location, scan addresses, or infer device details.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares four attacks against several address-generation methods and explains how using more than one address can change the privacy outcome.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7721 is an Informational analysis of trade-offs, not a protocol defining a new address-generation method. Temporary and stable opaque identifiers reduce some risks, but address use and operational needs still matter.

sections.title: Interface Identifiers and Address Stability
sections.content:
In IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration, routers advertise a prefix and a host generates an Interface Identifier (IID) to complete its address. IIDs can be manually configured, derived from an IEEE hardware identifier, generated cryptographically, or generated as stable opaque or temporary values. DHCPv6 and transition technologies provide other possibilities.

The RFC distinguishes a stable address, which does not vary over time on one IPv6 link, from a temporary address, which does. A constant IID remains the same across links, while a stable IID can stay the same only within a defined context, such as one link. Address stability and whether an address is publicly linked to another identifier are separate properties.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv6 host can build its interface identifier in several ways. Some identifiers stay the same across networks, while others change over time or when the host moves to a different link.

sections.title: Four Risks from Hardware-Based IIDs
sections.content:
The RFC describes four attacks involving IIDs derived from IEEE identifiers. Correlation links a device's activity over time because the identifier can last as long as its network interface. Location tracking uses the same IID to recognize a device after its IPv6 prefix changes.

Address scanning can exploit the structured bits in a hardware-derived IID, including the 24-bit OUI and fixed 0xff, 0xfe bytes in Modified EUI-64. Device-specific exploitation can use the address to infer information such as the network-card vendor or software type. The first three attacks require the attacker to learn the IID first.
sections.plainLanguage: A hardware-derived IID can link a device's activity over time and across networks. Its structure can also make addresses easier to scan and may reveal details about the device.

sections.title: Comparing Address-Generation Methods
sections.content:
The RFC's comparison table shows that IEEE-identifier IIDs are exposed to all four attacks. Constant semantically opaque IIDs prevent address scanning and device-specific exploitation but still permit correlation and location tracking. Cryptographically generated addresses prevent location tracking, scanning, and device-specific exploitation, but correlation can continue while the public key and modifier block remain in use.

Stable semantically opaque IIDs are generated per IPv6 link. They prevent location tracking, address scanning, and device-specific exploitation, while correlation can continue within one link. A host using only temporary IIDs limits correlation to the lifetime of a temporary address and prevents the other three attacks based on the IID.

Combining addresses matters. A host that also configures a hardware-based IID can remain exposed even if it sends outbound traffic using temporary addresses, because an attacker can probe for the stable IID. Publishing both a stable and temporary address where they can be linked also makes activity correlatable.
sections.plainLanguage: Opaque identifiers can prevent address scanning and device profiling, and per-link identifiers can also reduce tracking across networks. A second, more revealing address can undo some of those gains even if the host usually sends from a temporary address.

sections.title: DHCP, Transition Methods, and Operations
sections.content:
DHCPv6 address privacy depends on whether the client requests a temporary or non-temporary address and on the server implementation. Randomly leased non-temporary addresses can be stable and opaque; sequential addresses can follow patterns that make scanning easier. Transition methods that embed an IPv4 address inherit privacy properties from that address. The RFC notes that Teredo implementations added 12 random bits, later standardized in RFC 5991.

Addresses that change over time can make logging, troubleshooting, access control, and quality-of-service enforcement more complex. Some organizations disable temporary addresses despite the privacy cost. The RFC also recommends that IPv6 compliance tests not require hardware-derived identifiers when other, more privacy-friendly address methods are used.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 privacy depends on how its server chooses addresses, and some transition addresses reveal information from IPv4. Frequently changing addresses can also make network operations harder.

sections.title: Limits of the Comparison
sections.content:
The RFC's security considerations are its analysis of address-generation privacy and security. Its summary table evaluates attacks based on the IID, but a host may remain vulnerable through other protocols or identifiers.

The analysis also assumes that IPv6 prefixes are shared by a reasonably large number of nodes. When very few nodes use a prefix for a long time, the prefix itself may help correlate activity regardless of IID choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing an IID does not prevent tracking through other identifiers such as cookies or account names. A prefix used by very few hosts can also reveal activity, regardless of the IID method.
